text: For two decades the Hyde Park House was the center of everything.
In 1860, on his grand North American tour, the young Prince of Wales, the future Edward the Seventh, dined there.
The hotel hosted the affluent and the visiting and the merely curious.
Then in the summer of 1865 it took in its most famous and most sorrowful guest.
Mary Todd Lincoln came to the Hyde Park House with her sons Robert and Tad, only a few months after her husband was shot in Washington.
The lake was meant to offer some quiet for a grief nobody could fix.
She stayed about two and a half months before moving downtown.
Think about that picture for a moment.
The widow of the murdered president, sitting out the worst summer of her life in a half-built suburb that barely existed a decade earlier.
It is as good a marker as any of how fast this place had arrived.
The hotel itself did not last.
It burned to the ground in a fire in 1879.
The town grew up around the station and the hotel.
By 1861 the residents petitioned to organize as Hyde Park Township, and Cornell served as its first town supervisor.
He kept buying and shaping land, and the township he helped govern eventually sprawled across dozens of square miles of the South Side, far past the original 300 acres.
He was not only selling lots.

He pushed for parks, served years on the South Park commission, and helped bring the great pleasure grounds that Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux would lay out in Jackson and Washington Parks, just south and west of his land.
The parks were good civic work, and they were also good for the value of everything nearby.
With Cornell, the two were rarely far apart.
